summary: Updates RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 by defining code points for the 6LoWPAN ESC dispatch type and listing registration entries for known use cases.

eli5.summary: 6LoWPAN has an escape door for extra features that was never explained. This explains how it works and lists its first uses.

questions: what is the 6lowpan esc dispatch type
what is an esc extension type
what happens to an unknown esc extension type
how are esc extension types registered
subtitle: Gives the 6LoWPAN escape dispatch type a defined layout and a registry for the extensions that use it.

tldr.problem: 6LoWPAN headers have an ESC dispatch type for extra dispatch octets, but neither RFC 4944 nor RFC 6282 said what the octets after it mean, and groups had started using them anyway.
tldr.mechanism: The first octet after ESC becomes an ESC Extension Type (EET) with values 0 to 255, a new IANA registry tracks the values, and rules say how nodes treat unknown types.
tldr.outcome: Extensions can now be registered without clashing, and they must not change how existing dispatch types behave. This RFC updates RFC 4944 and RFC 6282.

today: RFC 8066 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4944 and RFC 6282.

sections.title: The Undefined Escape Hatch
sections.content:
Section 5.1 of RFC 4944 defines the 6LoWPAN dispatch header and its types. One of them, the ESC type, exists so that additional dispatch octets can follow in the header. RFC 6282 changed the value of the ESC dispatch type, and IANA recorded that value.

What neither RFC defined was the octets that come after ESC or how to use them. Meanwhile, implementations and standards bodies had started using those octets. This document updates both RFCs by defining the extension octet code points and creating a new "ESC Extension Types" registry, and it records one existing use from ITU-T.
sections.eli5: There was a door marked ESC for extra features, but no sign saying what was behind it. People started walking through anyway, so this RFC writes the sign.

sections.title: The ESC Frame Format
sections.content:
The ESC dispatch type is the left-most octet and holds 01000000. The first octet after it is the ESC Extension Type (EET). It selects which extension is in use. Everything after the EET is the Extended Dispatch Payload (EDP), and the extension itself decides how the EDP is laid out.

EET values run from 0 to 255. Values 0 and 255 are reserved for future use, and IANA assigns 1 to 254. EET values behave like dispatch values but come after the ESC type, so the two use orthogonal code spaces. Multiple ESC dispatch types MAY appear in one 6LoWPAN header, though the RFC calls that not desirable.

Each extension type needs a specification that defines its payload. Such specifications MUST NOT redefine existing EET codes, and a new EET MUST NOT modify the behavior of existing dispatch types from RFC 4944.
sections.eli5: After the ESC door comes a number saying which extra feature you want. Whatever follows that number belongs to that feature. Nobody may reuse a number or change what the old doors do.

sections.title: Unknown Extensions and Older Nodes
sections.content:
Existing RFC 4944 implementations cannot process ESC extension data. The RFC expects that such a node will drop the packet or ignore the ESC dispatch octets when it meets an EET it does not know.

An implementation that follows this document MUST drop a packet when it reaches an EET it does not understand. A router node SHOULD still forward a 6LoWPAN packet carrying EET octets, as long as it does not try to process the unknown extension.

Placement matters. ESC dispatch types can be first, last or in the middle. A node that does not understand the EET at the start of the packet drops it. Putting the EET later gives a legacy device a chance to recognize and handle an earlier dispatch type, and then ignore the EET instead of dropping the whole packet.
sections.eli5: If you find a door you do not understand, a new-style node throws the packet away, but a router may still pass it along unopened. Putting the strange door near the back means older nodes can read the front part first.

sections.title: Where ESC Goes in a Packet
sections.content:
When a LOWPAN_IPHC dispatch type is present, ESC dispatch types MUST appear before it, to stay backward compatible with Section 3.2 of RFC 6282. The RFC shows several typical orderings:

  • ESC, EET, EDP, then the dispatch, the LOWPAN_IPHC header and the payload.
  • A mesh header, then ESC, EET and EDP, then the dispatch and LOWPAN_IPHC header.
  • A mesh header followed by ESC, EET and EDP alone.
  • A mesh header and fragment header followed by ESC, EET and EDP.
  • ESC, EET and EDP as the whole 6LoWPAN encapsulation.

One known user is ITU-T G.9903 (G3-PLC), which uses the ESC dispatch type for native mesh routing and bootstrapping. Its command IDs are formatted like EET fields and run from 0x01 to 0x1F.

The RFC also clarifies NALP dispatch codes, which mark non-6LoWPAN payloads. They only provide that escape when they are the initial octet of a LoWPAN encapsulation. Their meaning anywhere else is reserved for future use, and ESC types are orthogonal to them.
sections.eli5: The ESC piece can sit in different spots in the packet, but if there is a compressed IPv6 header, ESC must come first. One power-line system already uses it for its own commands.

sections.title: The ESC Extension Types Registry
sections.content:
IANA registered the "ESC Extension Types" values under the Specification Required policy, the same policy as in RFC 4944. A Designated Expert reviews the public specification that requests a value. Each specification MUST define the Extended Dispatch Payload octets so receivers can read the ESC types interoperably, and it MUST say how the ESC octets are used with 6LoWPAN headers.

The code points MUST be used with 6lo protocols that follow RFC 4944 or its derivatives. The initial registry holds value 0 and 255 as reserved, values 1 to 31 for ITU-T G.9903 and G.9905 command IDs, and 32 to 254 unassigned.
sections.eli5: To get a number, you write a public document explaining your feature, and an expert checks it. At the start, a few numbers are saved for a power-line standard and the rest are free.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no additional security threats from the ESC dispatch assignments it describes. It also forbids defining any extended dispatch values or extension types that modify the behavior of existing dispatch types, which keeps new extensions from changing how current header types are treated.
sections.eli5: Adding a labeled door adds no new danger, and the rules say new doors may not change how old ones work.
